claim: The motor system has a remarkable ability to adapt to novel environments.
source: The remarkable ability of the motor system to adapt to novel environments has traditionally been investigated using kinematically non-redundant tasks, such as planar reaching movements.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus in motor control research.

claim: Motor adaptation has traditionally been investigated using kinematically non-redundant tasks such as planar reaching movements.
source: The remarkable ability of the motor system to adapt to novel environments has traditionally been investigated using kinematically non-redundant tasks, such as planar reaching movements.
evidence: This statement reflects established research practices in the field.

claim: Traditional non-redundant tasks prevent the study of how the motor system achieves adaptation by altering movement patterns of redundant body systems.
source: This limitation prevents the study of how the motor system achieves adaptation by altering the movement patterns of our redundant body.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of previous experimental approaches.

claim: A redundant motor task was developed in which participants reached for targets with the tip of a virtual stick held with both hands.
source: To address this issue, we developed a redundant motor task in which participants reached for targets with the tip of a virtual stick held with both hands.
evidence: This describes the experimental method developed in the study.

claim: Participants consistently employed a stereotypical strategy of flexibly changing the tilt angle of the stick depending on the direction of tip movement.
source: Despite the redundancy of the task, participants consistently employed a stereotypical strategy of flexibly changing the tilt angle of the stick depending on the direction of tip movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations reported in the study.

claim: The baseline relationship between tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle constrained both the physical and visual movement patterns of the redundant system.
source: Thus, this baseline relationship between tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle constrained both the physical and visual movement patterns of the redundant system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing stereotypical movement patterns.

claim: Both tip-movement direction perturbations and stick-tilt angle perturbations drove adaptation.
source: Both types of perturbations, whether directly affecting the task (tip-movement direction) or not (stick-tilt angle around the tip), drove adaptation, and the patterns of implicit adaptation were guided by the baseline relationship.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Patterns of implicit adaptation were guided by the baseline relationship between tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle.
source: Both types of perturbations, whether directly affecting the task (tip-movement direction) or not (stick-tilt angle around the tip), drove adaptation, and the patterns of implicit adaptation were guided by the baseline relationship.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations showing adaptation patterns following the baseline TMD-STA relationship.

claim: Tip-movement adaptation was associated with changes in stick-tilt angle.
source: Consequently, tip-movement adaptation was associated with changes in stick-tilt angle, and intriguingly, even seemingly ignorable stick-tilt perturbations significantly influenced tip-movement adaptation, leading to tip-movement direction errors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Stick-tilt perturbations significantly influenced tip-movement adaptation, leading to tip-movement direction errors.
source: Consequently, tip-movement adaptation was associated with changes in stick-tilt angle, and intriguingly, even seemingly ignorable stick-tilt perturbations significantly influenced tip-movement adaptation, leading to tip-movement direction errors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The baseline relationship plays a crucial role in how the motor system controls movement of the redundant system.
source: These findings provide a new understanding that the baseline relationship plays a crucial role not only in how the motor system controls movement of the redundant system, but also in how it implicitly adapts to modify movement patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The baseline relationship plays a crucial role in how the motor system implicitly adapts to modify movement patterns.
source: These findings provide a new understanding that the baseline relationship plays a crucial role not only in how the motor system controls movement of the redundant system, but also in how it implicitly adapts to modify movement patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The motor system automatically and implicitly updates motor commands to reduce movement errors.
source: If a movement error occurs while reaching a target, the motor system automatically and implicitly updates the motor command for the next movement to reduce the error.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in motor learning research.

claim: Motor learning ability contributes to maintaining accurate movements in the presence of noise.
source: This remarkable motor learning ability contributes not only to maintaining accurate movements in the presence of noise but also to flexibly adapting the movement to new environments.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of motor learning functions.

claim: Motor learning ability contributes to flexibly adapting movement to new environments.
source: This remarkable motor learning ability contributes not only to maintaining accurate movements in the presence of noise but also to flexibly adapting the movement to new environments.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of motor learning functions.

claim: In the standard planar arm-reaching task, participants manipulate a visual cursor with their hands primarily by moving their shoulder and elbow joints.
source: In the standard planar arm-reaching task, which has been widely used to study the mechanisms of motor learning, participants manipulate a visual cursor with their hands primarily by moving their shoulder and elbow joints (Flash and Hogan, 1985; Gordon et al., 1994; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and Figure 1a.

claim: The arm-reaching task has contributed to uncovering many important properties of motor adaptation when a novel environment is introduced.
source: The arm-reaching task has contributed to uncovering many important properties of motor adaptation when a novel environment is introduced (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 1999; Mazzoni and Krakauer, 2006; Taylor and Ivry, 2011; Takiyama et al., 2015; Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There is no redundancy between hand position and joint angles in the planar arm-reaching task.
source: Notably, there is no redundancy between hand position and joint angles in such a planar arm-reaching task.
evidence: This is a kinematic fact about two-joint planar reaching.

claim: Joint angles are primarily determined by the target to be reached in planar arm-reaching tasks.
source: The joint angles are primarily determined by the target to be reached (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by kinematic principles and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: When the motor system adapts reaching movement to visual rotation, the adapted pattern of joint angles is determined.
source: Because of this non-redundancy, when the motor system adapts the reaching movement to the visual rotation imposed on the cursor (Figure 1c, left), the adapted pattern of joint angles is also determined (Figure 1c, right).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of non-redundancy, illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: The adapted pattern of joint angles should be identical to the pattern when reaching in the adapted direction.
source: Naturally, the adapted pattern of joint angles should be identical to the pattern when reaching in the adapted direction (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a logical inference from non-redundancy, illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: Body systems for performing practical motor tasks generally have more degrees of freedom than necessary to accomplish the tasks.
source: However, our body systems for performing practical motor tasks generally have more degrees of freedom than necessary to accomplish the tasks (Bernstein et al., 1996; Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on motor redundancy.

claim: In golf swing, there are countless patterns of whole-body configurations to achieve identical clubhead positions at ball contact.
source: For example, in the golf swing, there are countless patterns of whole-body configurations to achieve identical clubhead positions at ball contact.
evidence: This is an example illustrating motor redundancy in a real-world task.

claim: The motor system solves task redundancy by minimizing motor cost.
source: However, given that the motor system solves task redundancy by minimizing motor cost (Collins, 1995; O'Sullivan et al., 2009) or movement error (White and Diedrichsen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2018), we should observe a stereotypical pattern of joint angles according to the targets (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on motor optimization.

claim: The motor system solves task redundancy by minimizing movement error.
source: However, given that the motor system solves task redundancy by minimizing motor cost (Collins, 1995; O'Sullivan et al., 2009) or movement error (White and Diedrichsen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2018), we should observe a stereotypical pattern of joint angles according to the targets (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on motor optimization.

claim: Stereotypical patterns of joint angles should be observed according to targets when the motor system solves task redundancy.
source: However, given that the motor system solves task redundancy by minimizing motor cost (Collins, 1995; O'Sullivan et al., 2009) or movement error (White and Diedrichsen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2018), we should observe a stereotypical pattern of joint angles according to the targets (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a prediction based on optimization principles, illustrated in Figure 1g.

claim: It has not been thoroughly investigated how the motor system coordinates to change the redundant body system to implicitly adapt to perturbations to the cursor representing the position of the end-effector.
source: It has not been thoroughly investigated how the motor system coordinates to change the redundant body system to implicitly adapt to the perturbation to the cursor representing the position of the end-effector.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature.

claim: Previous studies have consistently shown that the motor system actively corrects for task-relevant variability while allowing task-irrelevant variability.
source: Previous studies have consistently shown that the motor system actively corrects for task-relevant variability while allowing task-irrelevant variability (Mosier et al., 2005; Latash, 2012; van Beers et al., 2013; Sternad, 2018; Scholz and Schöner, 1999; Scholz et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Optimal feedback control theory suggests that strategies based on the minimal intervention principle are optimal in terms of achieving task goals.
source: Optimal feedback control theory suggests that the strategies based on such a 'minimal intervention principle' are optimal in terms of achieving task goals (e.g. movement accuracy; Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Todorov, 2004; Scott, 2004; Diedrichsen, 2007; Valero-Cuevas et al., 2009; Ronsse et al., 2010; Sternad et al., 2011; Selgrade and Chang, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The motor system does not intervene in movement change or variability as long as the task goal is achieved.
source: These studies demonstrated that the motor system does not intervene movement change or variability as long as the task goal is achieved.
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous studies on task-relevant and task-irrelevant variability.

claim: The motor system should ignore perturbations to joint angles that do not affect the task goal according to minimal intervention principle.
source: Thus, the motor system should ignore the perturbations to joint angles that do not affect the task goal (Figure 1k, left).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the minimal intervention principle, illustrated in Figure 1k.

claim: Previous studies did not directly test whether the redundant body movement pattern is unchanged when the end-effector movement remains unchanged.
source: However, these studies did not directly test whether the redundant body movement pattern is also unchanged when the end-effector movement remains unchanged.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in previous research.

claim: The motor system adapts to change the movement in response to task-irrelevant perturbations.
source: Conversely, it has also been reported that the motor system adapts to change the movement in response to the task-irrelevant perturbation (Wolpert et al., 1995; Flanagan and Rao, 1995; Morehead et al., 2017; Diedrichsen et al., 2010; Schaefer et al., 2012; Franklin et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: When the cursor trajectory was curved only in the middle of the reaching movement, the hand movement was adaptively modified even though the perturbation did not cause a reaching error at the target.
source: For example, when the cursor trajectory was curved only in the middle of the reaching movement, the hand movement was adaptively modified even though the perturbation did not cause a reaching error at the target (Wolpert et al., 1995; Flanagan and Rao, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific experimental findings.

claim: Previous studies created the task-irrelevant condition by applying the perturbation to the end-effector.
source: It should be noted that these previous studies created the task-irrelevant condition by applying the perturbation to the end-effector.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous experimental approaches.

claim: The current study focuses on how the motor system responds to the perturbation of the redundant body while the end-effector remains unaffected.
source: In contrast, the present study focuses on how the motor system responds to the perturbation of the redundant body while the end-effector remains unaffected (Figure 1i and Figure 1k).
evidence: This describes the novel approach of the current study.

claim: A novel bimanual stick manipulation task was introduced to investigate how the motor system adapts the redundant body system to perturbations.
source: To investigate the problem of how the motor system adapts the redundant body system to these perturbations, this study introduces a novel bimanual stick manipulation task specifically designed to address this issue (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the experimental method developed in the study.

claim: Participants manipulated a virtual stick held with both hands to reach visual targets by the tip of the stick.
source: Participants manipulated a virtual stick held with both hands to reach visual targets by the tip of the stick.
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: Redundancy in the task is achieved by acknowledging that the same tip position can be achieved with different stick angles.
source: Redundancy in the task is achieved by acknowledging that the same tip position can be achieved with different stick angles (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a kinematic property of the task, illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: The task allowed visual perturbation of the tip position (end-effector relevant perturbation).
source: Importantly, this task allowed us to visually perturb the tip position (i.e. end-effector relevant perturbation) and the stick angle (i.e. end-effector irrelevant perturbation) either separately or simultaneously.
evidence: This describes a capability of the experimental design.

claim: The task allowed visual perturbation of the stick angle (end-effector irrelevant perturbation).
source: Importantly, this task allowed us to visually perturb the tip position (i.e. end-effector relevant perturbation) and the stick angle (i.e. end-effector irrelevant perturbation) either separately or simultaneously.
evidence: This describes a capability of the experimental design.

claim: A total of 72 healthy participants took part in the study across Experiments 1-3.
source: A total of 72 healthy participants took part in the study (Experiments 1–3).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental sample.

claim: Participants were asked to manipulate a virtual stick with both hands (length = 40 cm; distance between hands = 15 cm) to move the right tip of the stick towards the targets.
source: They were asked to manipulate a virtual stick with both hands (length = 40 cm; distance between hands = 15 cm) to move the right tip of the stick towards the targets (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the experimental task parameters.

claim: The task is redundant because the same target can be reached in countless movement patterns.
source: This task is redundant because the same target can be reached in countless movement patterns.
evidence: This is a kinematic property of the task design.

claim: Participants could move both hands in parallel without tilting the stick.
source: The participants could move both hands in parallel without tilting the stick (Figure 2b, top).
evidence: This describes one possible strategy for the task, illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: Participants could perform the task by tilting the stick.
source: Alternatively, they could perform the task by tilting the stick (Figure 2b, bottom).
evidence: This describes an alternative strategy for the task, illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: During the baseline phase (360 trials), participants moved the tip from a starting point to a target (movement distance = 10 cm) that appeared in one of nine directions (0°, ±10°, ±20°, ±30°, and ±40°).
source: During the first part of the task (baseline phase: 360 trials) in all the experiments (Experiments 1–3), the participants moved the tip from a starting point to a target (movement distance = 10 cm) that appeared in one of nine directions (0°: horizontal direction,±10°,±20°,±30°, and ±40°; Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes the baseline experimental protocol.

claim: The trajectories of the tip and both hands appeared to be almost straight.
source: The trajectories of the tip and both hands appeared to be almost straight, but both hands were not moved in parallel, except when aiming at the 0° target (Figure 2d, top).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Both hands were not moved in parallel, except when aiming at the 0° target.
source: The trajectories of the tip and both hands appeared to be almost straight, but both hands were not moved in parallel, except when aiming at the 0° target (Figure 2d, top).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The velocity profiles of the hands and tip were bell-shaped, similar to a normal unimanual reaching movement.
source: The velocity profiles of the hands and tip were bell-shaped (Figure 2d, bottom), similar to a normal unimanual reaching movement (Flash and Hogan, 1985; Gordon et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2d and citations to previous research.

claim: Participants moved the tip while slightly tilting the stick, except when aiming at the 0° target.
source: The time-course changes in the stick-tilt angle relative to the initial horizontal tilt angle showed that the participants moved the tip while slightly tilting the stick, except when aiming at the 0° target (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The tendency to tilt the stick was observed from the beginning of the experiment (t-test compared with 0°, |t(71)|>6.4, Bonferroni corrected p<0.001).
source: This tendency was observed from the beginning of the experiment (t-test compared with 0°, |t(71)|>6.4, Bonferroni corrected p<0.001; Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: All participants showed stereotypical movement patterns where the stick-tilt angle was significantly modulated by the tip-movement direction.
source: Although each participant could have performed the task differently (Figure 2b), all participants showed stereotypical movement patterns: The stick-tilt angle was significantly modulated by the tip-movement direction (t-test compared with 0°, |t(71)|>5.5, Bonferroni corrected p<0.01; Figure 3a, inset).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Clockwise tip movement direction was accompanied by clockwise stick-tilt.
source: The relationship showed that clockwise (CW) tip movement direction was accompanied by CW stick-tilt, and counterclockwise (CCW) tip-movement direction was accompanied by CCW stick-tilt.
evidence: This is an observation from the baseline TMD-STA relationship shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Counterclockwise tip-movement direction was accompanied by counterclockwise stick-tilt.
source: The relationship showed that clockwise (CW) tip movement direction was accompanied by CW stick-tilt, and counterclockwise (CCW) tip-movement direction was accompanied by CCW stick-tilt.
evidence: This is an observation from the baseline TMD-STA relationship shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The constraint of movement patterns was likely created by minimizing the movement distance of the hands.
source: This constraint of movement patterns was likely created by minimizing the movement distance of the hands.
evidence: This is an inference based on optimization principles and supported by the data in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: If both hands are moved in parallel, the total distance between the initial and final positions of the hands should be 20 cm (10 cm for each) regardless of the targets.
source: If both hands are moved in parallel, the total distance between the initial and final positions of the hands should be 20 cm (10 cm for each) regardless of the targets; however, the experimentally observed distance was reduced by tilting the stick (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a kinematic calculation illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: The experimentally observed distance was reduced by tilting the stick.
source: If both hands are moved in parallel, the total distance between the initial and final positions of the hands should be 20 cm (10 cm for each) regardless of the targets; however, the experimentally observed distance was reduced by tilting the stick (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The average distance was a near-minimal value (versus parallel translation: Cohen's d=1.914, versus theoretical minimum: Cohen's d=0.334).
source: The average distance was a near-minimal value (versus parallel translation: Cohen's d=1.914, versus theoretical minimum: Cohen's d=0.334; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In Experiment 1A (N=19), the tip-movement direction was visually rotated in the CCW direction around the starting position (tip perturbation), whereas the stick-tilt angle remained unchanged.
source: In Experiment 1 A (N=19), the tip-movement direction was visually rotated in the CCW direction around the starting position (tip perturbation), whereas the stick-tilt angle remained unchanged (Figure 4a).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 1A.

claim: The tip perturbation produced a positional dissociation between vision (the stick) and proprioception (the hands).
source: Thus, this perturbation produced a positional dissociation between vision (i.e. the stick) and proprioception (i.e. the hands).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The amount of tip directional rotation was gradually increased by 1° per trial up to 30° so that the participants did not notice the presence of perturbation.
source: The amount of tip directional rotation was gradually increased by 1° per a trial up to 30° so that the participants did not notice the presence of perturbation.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Experiment 1A.

claim: The participants adapted to the tip perturbation by tilting the stick.
source: The experimental results demonstrated that the participants adapted to the tip perturbation by tilting the stick (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: After adaptation, the tip-movement direction remained at the baseline level (paired t-test, t(18) = –1.320, p=0.203).
source: On the visual plane (Figure 5a), after the adaptation, the tip-movement direction remained at the baseline level (paired t-test, t(18) = –1.320, p=0.203), while the stick was tilted significantly more in the CW direction than when aiming at the 0° target in the baseline phase (paired t-test, t(18) = 10.003, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: After adaptation, the stick was tilted significantly more in the CW direction than when aiming at the 0° target in the baseline phase (paired t-test, t(18) = 10.003, p<0.01).
source: On the visual plane (Figure 5a), after the adaptation, the tip-movement direction remained at the baseline level (paired t-test, t(18) = –1.320, p=0.203), while the stick was tilted significantly more in the CW direction than when aiming at the 0° target in the baseline phase (paired t-test, t(18) = 10.003, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The tip perturbation was compensated by adaptation, but the adaptation produced an abnormal visual stick-tilt.
source: Thus, the tip perturbation was compensated by adaptation, but the adaptation produced an abnormal visual stick-tilt.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Experiment 1A.

claim: Participants ignored the abnormal visual stick-tilt which did not directly influence the task, supporting the minimal intervention principle.
source: This result is likely to support the idea of the minimal intervention principle because participants ignored this visual stick-tilt which did not directly influence the task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in relation to theoretical predictions.

claim: On the physical plane, adaptation appeared to progress along the baseline TMD–STA relationship throughout the adaptation phase.
source: On the physical plane, adaptation appeared to progress along the baseline TMD–STA relationship throughout the adaptation phase (Figure 5b and Figure 5c).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: The implicitly adapted tip-movement direction was similar to that when voluntarily aiming at the –30° target in the baseline phase, although the difference was small but significant (paired t-test, t(18) = –10.053, p<0.01).
source: The implicitly adapted tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle were similar to those when voluntarily aiming at the –30° target in the baseline phase. Although the difference was small but significant for the tip-movement direction (paired t-test, t(18) = –10.053, p<0.01), there was no significant difference in the stick-tilt angle (paired t-test, t(18) = –1.081, p=0.294).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in the stick-tilt angle between the adapted pattern and the baseline pattern when aiming at the –30° target (paired t-test, t(18) = –1.081, p=0.294).
source: The implicitly adapted tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle were similar to those when voluntarily aiming at the –30° target in the baseline phase. Although the difference was small but significant for the tip-movement direction (paired t-test, t(18) = –10.053, p<0.01), there was no significant difference in the stick-tilt angle (paired t-test, t(18) = –1.081, p=0.294).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The motor system implicitly achieved adaptation to the tip perturbation as if it had voluntarily aimed at the –30° target.
source: Thus, the motor system implicitly achieved adaptation to the tip perturbation as if it had voluntarily aimed at the –30° target (i.e. pattern ii in Figure 4c and Figure 4d; Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Participants who showed a larger stick-tilt when aiming at the –30° target during the baseline phase also exhibited a larger stick-tilt in the adapted pattern (R=0.601, p=0.007).
source: This adaptation characteristic was also supported by the observation that the participants who tilted their stick more when aiming at the –30° target in the baseline phase exhibited a greater stick-tilt in the adapted movement patterns (R=0.601, p=0.007; Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: In Experiment 1B (N=13), a 30° tip perturbation was imposed abruptly to allow participants to use explicit strategy, and nearly identical results to Experiment 1A were obtained.
source: In Experiment 1B (N=13), we imposed the 30° tip perturbation abruptly to allow participants to use explicit strategy, and obtained nearly identical results (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation and results of Experiment 1B.

claim: The adapted tip-movement direction on the physical plane was significantly different from the tip-movement direction when aiming at the –30° target in the baseline phase in Experiment 1A.
source: As described above, the adapted tip-movement direction on the physical plane was significantly different from the tip-movement direction when aiming at the –30° target in the baseline phase (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Such significant difference in tip-movement direction was not observed for Experiment 1B.
source: In contrast, such significant difference was not observed for Experiment 1B (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference in tip-movement direction in Experiment 1A was caused by implicit adaptation to correct the abnormal visual stick-tilt angle.
source: We speculated that this difference was caused by the implicit adaptation to correct the abnormal visual stick-tilt angle.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the difference between Experiment 1A and 1B.

claim: If the physical movement pattern is constrained by the baseline TMD–STA relationship, the CCW correction of the stick-tilt angle should be accompanied by the CCW change in tip-movement, which would interfere with the adaptation to the tip perturbation.
source: If the physical movement pattern is constrained by the baseline TMD–STA relationship, the CCW correction of the stick-tilt angle should be accompanied by the CCW change in tip-movement, which would interfere with the adaptation to the tip perturbation.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the baseline TMD-STA relationship.

claim: Experiment 2 (N=20) was designed to directly test whether the motor system corrects for stick-tilt error that does not directly influence the tip position.
source: Thus, it is still possible that the motor system does not necessarily ignore,but corrects for, the stick-tilt error that does not directly influence the tip position. Experiment 2 (N=20) was designed to directly test this possibility by imposing a stick-tilt perturbation around the right tip (i.e., end-effector irrelevant perturbation) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This describes the rationale and design of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, as the tip moved from the starting point, the stick started to tilt around the tip up to ±6° when the tip reached the target.
source: As the tip moved from the starting point, the stick started to tilt around the tip up to ±6° when the tip reached the target (the tilt amount was proportional to the tip's distance from the starting point).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 2.

claim: The ±6° tilt perturbation was chosen according to the stick tilt at the movement offset when reaching the ±30° target for the baseline phase.
source: The ±6° tilt perturbation was chosen according to the stick tilt at the movement offset when reaching the ±30° target for the baseline phase (see Figure 3a).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the perturbation magnitude.

claim: Ten participants participated in the CCW stick-tilt perturbation condition (E2CCW group: 6°), and the remaining ten participants took part in the CW stick-tilt perturbation condition (E2CW group: –6°).
source: Ten participants participated in the CCW stick-tilt perturbation condition (E2CCW group: 6°), and the remaining ten participants took part in the CW stick-tilt perturbation condition (E2CW group: –6°).
evidence: This describes the experimental groups in Experiment 2.

claim: Because the perturbation amount was small, the participants did not notice the presence of perturbation throughout the experiment.
source: Because the amount was small, the participants did not notice the presence of perturbation throughout the experiment.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental manipulation.

claim: According to the minimal intervention principle, the motor system does not need to change anything because the stick-tilt perturbation does not affect the tip position.
source: According to the minimal intervention principle, the motor system does not need to change anything because the stick-tilt perturbation does not affect the tip position (i.e. the task goal; Figure 6c and Figure 6d, pattern i).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the minimal intervention principle.

claim: If the motor system is actively compensating for the stick-tilt perturbation, it should change the stick-tilt angle.
source: However, if the motor system is actively compensating for the stick-tilt perturbation, it should change the stick-tilt angle (Figure 6c and Figure 6d, pattern ii).
evidence: This is an alternative prediction to the minimal intervention principle.

claim: Participants corrected the stick-tilt angle in response to end-effector irrelevant perturbations.
source: Interestingly, the participants corrected the stick-tilt angle (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: On the visual plane, the stick-tilt angles remained different from those in the baseline phase (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, significant main effect of groups: F(1,18) = 54.457, p<0.001).
source: On the visual plane, the stick-tilt angles remained different from those in the baseline phase (Figure 7a; two-way (direction of stick-tilt perturbation [i.e. groups], trial phase [first 30 trials or last 30 trials])) repeated-measures ANOVA, a significant main effect of groups: F(1,18) = 54.457, p<0.001; no effect of trial phase: F(1,18) = 2.554, p=0.127; no interaction: F(1,18) = 1.613, p=0.220.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The adaptive changes did not fully compensate for the perturbation-induced stick-tilt errors.
source: Thus, the adaptive changes did not fully compensate for the perturbation-induced stick-tilt errors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis.

claim: Participants implicitly changed the stick-tilt angle in the direction opposite to that of the perturbation from the early adaptation phase.
source: However, the data on the physical plane clearly demonstrated that participants implicitly changed the stick-tilt angle in the direction opposite to that of the perturbation from the early adaptation phase (Figure 7b): Without the correction, the data of the E2CCW and E2CW groups should have largely overlapped.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: With respect to stick-tilt angle, two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed the main effect of stick-tilt perturbation direction (F(1, 18)=12.483, p<0.01) but not the main effect of trial phase (F(1, 18)=3.331, p=0.085).
source: However, with respect to stick-tilt angle, two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed the main effect of stick-tilt perturbation direction (F(1, 18)=12.483, p<0.01) but not the main effect of trial phase (F(1, 18)=3.331, p=0.085). The interaction between these factors was not significant (F(1, 18)=1.362, p=0.258).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Stick-tilt correction was accompanied by undesirable tip-movement directional errors.
source: Unexpectedly, this stick-tilt correction was accompanied by undesirable tip-movement directional errors (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: With respect to tip-movement direction, two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed the main effect of the direction of stick-tilt perturbation (F(1, 18)=5.104, p=0.037) but not the main effect of trial phase (F(1, 18)=1.288, p=0.271).
source: With respect to the tip-movement direction, two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed the main effect of the direction of stick-tilt perturbation (F(1, 18)=5.104, p=0.037) but not the main effect of trial phase (F(1, 18)=1.288, p=0.271) (the interaction between these factors was not significant: F(1, 18)=0.804, p=0.382).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The seemingly irrational adaptation patterns were consistent with the patterns predicted from the baseline physical TMD–STA relationship.
source: Notably, these seemingly irrational adaptation patterns were consistent with the patterns predicted from the baseline physical TMD–STA relationship: CCW (CW) stick-tilt adaptation to the CW (CCW) stick-tilt perturbation slightly shifted the tip-movement direction in the CCW (CW) direction (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in relation to the baseline relationship.

claim: A negative correlation was observed between the amount of stick-tilt correction and the amount of stick-tilt angle when aiming at the ±30° target in the baseline phase (R=–0.572, p<0.01).
source: As predicted, we observed a negative correlation (stick-tilt correction: R=–0.572, p<0.01; tip-movement directional change: R=–0.440, p=0.052), although the correlation for the tip-movement direction change was not significant.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The correlation between tip-movement directional change and baseline stick-tilt angle was not significant (R=–0.440, p=0.052).
source: As predicted, we observed a negative correlation (stick-tilt correction: R=–0.572, p<0.01; tip-movement directional change: R=–0.440, p=0.052), although the correlation for the tip-movement direction change was not significant.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The results of Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 suggest that implicit adaptation in the redundant stick-manipulating task is achieved by two mechanisms: the motor system attempts to correct for any perturbation in visual feedback, and the physical pattern of movement correction is constrained by the baseline TMD–STA relationship.
source: Taken together, the results of Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 suggest that the implicit adaptation in the redundant stick-manipulating task is achieved by the following two mechanisms: First, the motor system attempts to correct for any perturbation in visual feedback, regardless of whether it is end-effector relevant or end-effector irrelevant. Second, the physical pattern of movement correction is constrained by the baseline TMD–STA relationship.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Experiment 3 (N=20) was designed to investigate the interaction between adaptations to end-effector relevant and end-effector irrelevant perturbations by applying both simultaneously.
source: Experiment 3 (N=20) was designed to further investigate the interaction between adaptations to end-effector relevant and end-effector irrelevant perturbations by applying both simultaneously (Figure 8a).
evidence: This describes the rationale and design of Experiment 3.

claim: The CCW tip perturbation was combined with the CCW stick-tilt perturbation (E3CCW group: N=10) or with the CW stick-tilt perturbation (E3CW group: N=10).
source: Specifically, the CCW tip perturbation was combined with the CCW stick-tilt perturbation (E3CCW group: N=10) or with the CW stick-tilt perturbation (E3CW group: N=10).
evidence: This describes the experimental groups in Experiment 3.

claim: The correction pattern required for the E3CCW group is aligned with the baseline TMD–STA relationship, from which adaptation should proceed smoothly.
source: On the physical plane, the correction pattern required for the E3CCW group (Figure 8c, top) is aligned with the baseline TMD–STA relationship (green arrow in Figure 8d), from which we can predict that adaptation should proceed smoothly.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the baseline TMD-STA relationship.

claim: The correction pattern required for the E3CW group is orthogonal to the baseline TMD–STA relationship, which may prevent smooth adaptation.
source: In contrast, the correction pattern required for the E3CW group (Figure 8c, bottom) is orthogonal to the baseline TMD–STA relationship (orange arrow in Figure 8d), which may prevent smooth adaptation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the baseline TMD-STA relationship.

claim: The participants were unaware of the perturbations throughout Experiment 3.
source: Again, the participants were unaware of the perturbations throughout the experiment.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The difference in stick-tilt perturbation directions did not affect the final adapted movement patterns.
source: Contrary to the predictions, the difference in stick-tilt perturbation directions did not affect the final adapted movement patterns (Figure 9—figure supplement 1): As shown in the visual plane (Figure 9a), the difference in stick-tilt angle remained unchanged (paired t-test, t(18) = 6.920, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9a and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: On the physical plane, there were no significant differences in movement pattern between the two groups (tip-movement direction: paired t-test, t(18) = –0.479, p=0.638, stick-tilt angle: paired t-test, t(18) = –0.386, p=0.704).
source: Similarly, in the physical plane (Figure 9b), there were no significant differences in movement pattern between the two groups (tip-movement direction: paired t-test, t(18) = –0.479, p=0.638, stick-tilt angle: paired t-test, t(18) = –0.386, p=0.704).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: Trial-by-trial variability of the movement pattern in the latter adaptation phase (trial# 121–240) showed a slight difference between groups (t-test, tip-movement direction: t(18) = –2.046, p=0.056, stick-tilt angle, t(18) = –3.235, p=0.005).
source: However, a trial-by-trial variability of the movement pattern in the latter adaptation phase (trial# 121–240) showed a slight difference between groups (t-test, tip-movement direction: t(18) = –2.046, p=0.056, stick-tilt angle, t(18) = –3.235, p=0.005), suggesting that the adaptation processes were implicitly affected by combination of perturbations (Figure 9a, inset).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 9a inset.

claim: Two groups showed different adaptation processes with trial-dependent trajectories to the final adapted pattern clearly separated.
source: In partial agreement with our predictions, two groups showed different adaptation processes: trial-dependent trajectories to the final adapted pattern were clearly separated for both groups (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: A repeated-measures MANOVA showed a significant effect of group (Pillai's Trace F(8, 162)=0.155, p<0.001) and trial segment (Pillai's Trace F(8, 162)=0.719, p<0.001), but no significant interaction (Pillai's Trace F(8, 162)=0.039, p=0.982).
source: Indeed, a repeated-measures multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) showed a significant effect of group (Pillai's Trace F(8, 162)=0.155, p<0.001) and trial segment (Pillai's Trace F(8, 162)=0.719, p<0.001); however, no significant interaction was observed (Pillai's Trace F(8, 162)=0.039, p=0.982).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The adaptation of the tip movement was more delayed in the E3CW group (trial segment 2: t-test, t(18) = –3.684, Bonferroni-corrected p<0.05).
source: As a result, the adaptation of the tip movement was more delayed in the E3CW group (trial segment 2: t-test, t(18) = –3.684, Bonferroni-corrected p<0.05; Figure 9d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 9d.

claim: Understanding how the motor system resolves redundancy remains a challenging problem.
source: Our bodies have more degrees of freedom than necessary to achieve a relatively low-dimensional task goal. Understanding how the motor system resolves this redundancy remains a challenging problem (Bernstein et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to foundational work on motor redundancy.

claim: The study investigated how the motor system coordinates the redundant body movements to control the end-effector.
source: In this study, we investigated the problems of motor control and adaptation specific to kinematically redundant systems. The first problem is how the motor system coordinates the redundant body movements to control the end-effector (Figure 1f).
evidence: This describes one of the research questions addressed in the study.

claim: The study investigated how the motor system coordinates to modify redundant body movements when implicitly adapting to perturbations imposed on the end-effector.
source: The second problem is how the motor system coordinates to modify redundant body movements when implicitly adapting to the perturbation imposed on the end-effector (Figure 1i).
evidence: This describes another research question addressed in the study.

claim: The study investigated how the motor system responds to perturbations to the redundant dimension that do not directly affect the end-effector.
source: The third problem is how the motor system responds to the perturbation to the redundant dimension that does not directly affect the end-effector (Figure 1k).
evidence: This describes a third research question addressed in the study.

claim: Previous studies investigating task-irrelevant perturbations have applied perturbations to the end-effector without affecting task performance.
source: However, it should be noted that previous studies investigating the effect of task-irrelevant perturbations have applied perturbations to the end-effector (e.g. cursor) without affecting task performance (Wolpert et al., 1995; Flanagan and Rao, 1995; Diedrichsen et al., 2010; Schaefer et al., 2012; Franklin et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research approaches supported by citations.

claim: The present study focused on investigating the effect of perturbations on the redundant body while leaving the end-effector unaffected.
source: In contrast, the present study focused on investigating the effect of perturbations on the redundant body while leaving the end-effector unaffected (see Figure 1k).
evidence: This describes the novel approach of the current study.

claim: The study obtained four main results from experiments conducted with a specific configuration.
source: Because our experiments were conducted with a specific configuration (stick length, hand distance, target location etc), we must be cautious about the generalizability of the results to other configurations, but we obtained the following four main results.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations and introduces the main findings.

claim: Participants adopted a stereotyped strategy to reach the target with the stick tip, and the movement pattern was constrained by a baseline TMD–STA relationship.
source: First, we showed that participants adopted a stereotyped strategy to reach the target with the stick tip, and that the movement pattern (stick tip movement and stick tilt angle) was constrained by a baseline TMD–STA relationship.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the baseline phase.

claim: When only end-effector relevant perturbations were imposed on the tip, the motor system attempted to modify the physical movement patterns along the baseline TMD–STA relationship to achieve the task goal.
source: Second, when only end-effector relevant perturbations were imposed on the tip, the motor system attempted to modify the physical movement patterns along the baseline TMD–STA relationship to achieve the task goal (Experiment 1).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: When perturbations were applied only to the end-effector irrelevant dimension (stick-tilt angle), the motor system still adapted to the perturbation and this adaptation was accompanied by an end-effector relevant error.
source: Third, even when perturbations were applied only to the end-effector irrelevant dimension (i.e. the stick-tilt angle), the motor system still adapted to the end-effector irrelevant perturbation and this adaptation was accompanied by an end-effector relevant error (Experiment 2).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2.

claim: When both types of perturbations were imposed simultaneously, the adaptation processes were influenced depending on the combination of perturbations.
source: Finally, when both types of perturbations were imposed simultaneously, the adaptation processes were influenced depending on the combination of perturbations (Experiment 3).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 3.

claim: Stereotypical movement patterns have been reported for the movements of the joints in redundant three-dimensional reaching movements.
source: Such stereotypical movement patterns have been reported for the movements of the joints in the redundant three-dimensional reaching movements (Lacquaniti and Soechting, 1982; Proietti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Compared with the case where both hands moved in parallel, the movement distances of both hands to perform the task were significantly reduced to a near-optimal level.
source: Notably, compared with the case where both hands moved in parallel, the movement distances of both hands to perform the task were significantly reduced to a near-optimal level (Figure 3b and Figure 3c), which contributed to the reduction of work required (Collins, 1995; O'Sullivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and 3c, and citations to optimization principles.

claim: As a result of the optimization process, tip-movement and stick-tilt were associated with each other by the baseline TMD–STA relationship.
source: As a result of this optimization process, tip-movement and stick-tilt were associated with each other by the baseline TMD–STA relationship (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Physically, the baseline TMD-STA relationship constrains how the motor system should move the stick.
source: Physically, this relationship constrains how the motor system should move the stick.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of the baseline relationship.

claim: Visually, the baseline TMD-STA relationship tells the motor system how the stick movement should be seen.
source: Visually, it tells the motor system how the stick movement should be seen.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of the baseline relationship.

claim: The task has created redundancy in a natural way by using a bimanual stick manipulation task that is relatively common in everyday life.
source: Our task has several advantages. First, the task has created redundancy in a natural way. Manipulating a stick with both hands is relatively common in everyday life (using a broom, golf or bat swing etc.).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the experimental design.

claim: The familiarity with the task was reflected in the observation that all participants started tilting the stick to reach the tip toward the targets from the beginning of the experiment.
source: This familiarity with the task was reflected in Figure 2f which shows that all participants started tilting the stick to reach the tip toward the targets from the beginning of the experiment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The task allows investigation of how perturbation to the tip-movement direction leads to a change in both the tip-movement direction itself and the stick-tilt angle.
source: Second, this task allows us to investigate how the perturbation to the tip-movement direction leads to a change in both the tip-movement direction itself and the stick-tilt angle.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the experimental design.

claim: It has not been investigated how the motor system implicitly achieves adaptation to the end-effector perturbation by changing the movement patterns of the redundant body system.
source: It has not been investigated how the motor system implicitly achieves adaptation to the end-effector perturbation (i.e. the end-effector relevant perturbation) by changing the movement patterns of the redundant body system.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature.

claim: The task can create a novel condition in which perturbations are imposed on the redundant system while the tip position remains unchanged.
source: Third, this task can create a novel condition in which the perturbations are imposed on the redundant system while the tip position remains unchanged (i.e. the end-effector irrelevant perturbation).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the experimental design.

claim: No previous studies have investigated how the motor system implicitly responds to end-effector irrelevant perturbations by altering the movement of the redundant body system.
source: No previous studies have investigated how the motor system implicitly responds to such a perturbation by altering (or not altering) the movement of the redundant body system.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature.

claim: When the end-effector relevant perturbation was implicitly imposed to the tip-movement direction (visual rotation by 30° CCW), the participants adapted to change the tip-movement direction in the opposite CW direction.
source: When the end-effector relevant perturbation was implicitly imposed to the tip-movement direction (visual rotation by 30° CCW), the participants adapted to change the tip-movement direction in the opposite CW direction (Experiment 1), as reported in many previous studies using an ordinary reaching movement (Cunningham, 1989; Krakauer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 and citations to previous research.

claim: Participants implicitly corrected the tip-movement direction by changing the stick tilt as if they were voluntarily aiming at the –30° target.
source: Participants implicitly corrected the tip-movement direction by changing the stick tilt as if they were voluntarily aiming at the –30° target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of Experiment 1.

claim: The baseline TMD–STA relationship originally contributes to dictate how the motor system voluntarily moves the stick.
source: The baseline TMD–STA relationship originally contributes to dictate how the motor system voluntarily moves the stick.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of the baseline relationship.

claim: The motor system uses the baseline TMD-STA relationship as a scaffold to implicitly guide how to correct the tip-movement direction.
source: It is likely that the motor system also uses this relationship as a scaffold to implicitly guide how to correct the tip-movement direction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Hayashi et al., 2016 demonstrated that the adaptation of the standard reaching movement to a visual perturbation was significantly influenced by the baseline relationship between the movement and target directions (visuomotor map).
source: Hayashi et al., 2016 have demonstrated that the adaptation of the standard reaching movement to a visual perturbation was significantly influenced by the baseline relationship between the movement and target directions (i.e. a visuomotor map).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: After distorting the visuomotor map so that the movement direction was more (or less) sensitively modulated by the target direction, the movement adaptation was enhanced (or reduced).
source: After distorting the visuomotor map so that the movement direction was more (or less) sensitively modulated by the target direction, the movement adaptation was enhanced (or reduced).
evidence: This is a finding from Hayashi et al., 2016.

claim: The present finding that the baseline movement pattern is used for the implicit adaptation is consistent with the finding of Hayashi et al., 2016.
source: The present finding that the baseline movement pattern is used for the implicit adaptation is consistent with this previous finding.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous research.

claim: After adaptation, the amount of stick-tilt was equivalent to that when aiming at the –30° target.
source: However, after adaptation, the amount of stick-tilt was equivalent to that when aiming at the –30° target (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The visually observed stick-tilt after adaptation was different from that observed in the baseline condition.
source: Thus, the visually observed stick-tilt after adaptation was different from that observed in the baseline condition (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The adapted physical movement pattern persisted to follow the baseline TMD–STA relationship, suggesting that the motor system mainly paid attention to end-effector relevant tip-movement and ignored end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt angle.
source: Nevertheless, the adapted physical movement pattern persisted to follow the baseline TMD–STA relationship, suggesting that the motor system mainly paid attention to end-effector relevant tip-movement and ignored end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt angle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The adaptation pattern in Experiment 1A seems to be consistent with the minimal intervention principle.
source: This adaptation pattern seems to be consistent with the minimal intervention principle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in relation to theoretical predictions.

claim: A slight difference in the adaptation patterns between Experiment 1A and Experiment 1B implies a violation of the minimal intervention principle.
source: However, a slight difference in the adaptation patterns between Experiment 1 A and Experiment 1B implies a violation of the minimal intervention principle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences between experimental conditions.

claim: Visuomotor adaptation is often incomplete even after sufficient training, and residual errors are observed.
source: Visuomotor adaptation is often incomplete even after sufficient training, and residual errors are observed (Krakauer et al., 2000; Ethier et al., 2008; Malone et al., 2011; Vaswani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The presence of residual errors has been attributed to the imbalance between learning and forgetting.
source: Although the presence of residual errors has been attributed to the imbalance between learning and forgetting, a recent study demonstrated that only the implicit learning system is responsible for producing residual errors by modulating error sensitivity with the consistency of errors in previous trials (Albert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Only the implicit learning system is responsible for producing residual errors by modulating error sensitivity with the consistency of errors in previous trials.
source: Although the presence of residual errors has been attributed to the imbalance between learning and forgetting, a recent study demonstrated that only the implicit learning system is responsible for producing residual errors by modulating error sensitivity with the consistency of errors in previous trials (Albert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: An alternative mechanism involving correction of abnormal stick-tilt may be involved in the generation of residual difference in Experiment 1A.
source: We speculate that an alternative mechanism is involved in the generation of a residual difference in Experiment 1 A. If the motor system does not ignore the abnormal stick-tilt but attempts to correct it, and this correction pattern is physically constrained by the baseline TMD–STA relationship, the stick-tilt correction should accompany the de-adaptation of the tip-movement direction and lead to the generation of a residual error.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the experimental findings.

claim: The results of Experiment 2 and Experiment 3 support the idea that the motor system attempts to correct abnormal stick-tilt.
source: As discussed below, the results of Experiment 2 and Experiment 3 support this idea.
evidence: This is a forward reference to support for the speculation.

claim: Experiment 2 clearly demonstrated that the motor system responded to the stick-tilt perturbations, inconsistent with the minimal intervention principle.
source: However, inconsistent with this idea, Experiment 2 clearly demonstrated that the motor system responded to the stick-tilt perturbations (Figure 7b and Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and 7c.

claim: The motor system predicts the visual feedback of an end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt angle when performing the task and tries to eliminate the dissociation between the observed and predicted stick-tilt angle.
source: This result indicates that the motor system predicts the visual feedback of an end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt angle when performing the task and tries to eliminate the dissociation between the observed and predicted stick-tilt angle (i.e. sensory prediction error).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Participants who demonstrated a shallower TMD–STA relationship during the baseline phase showed a greater amount of stick-tilt correction.
source: This idea was corroborated by the fact that participants who demonstrated a shallower TMD–STA relationship during the baseline phase showed a greater amount of stick-tilt correction (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The ±6° stick-tilt perturbation should cause larger prediction error for participants with shallower TMD-STA relationship.
source: The ±6° stick-tilt perturbation should cause the larger prediction error for these participants.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the baseline relationship.

claim: Previous studies created task-irrelevant conditions by combining perturbation of visual cursors with manipulation of movement trajectory, target/cursor shape, or applying simultaneous equal perturbations to target and cursor.
source: These studies created the task-irrelevant condition by combining the perturbation of visual cursors with the manipulation of movement trajectory (Wolpert et al., 1995; Flanagan and Rao, 1995; Morehead et al., 2017), target/cursor shape (Diedrichsen et al., 2010; Schaefer et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2019), or applying the simultaneous equal perturbations to the target and cursor (Franklin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research approaches supported by citations.

claim: The perturbations in previous studies are not 'end-effector irrelevant' as defined in the current study.
source: Therefore, these perturbations are not 'end-effector irrelevant'.
evidence: This is a clarification of terminology in relation to previous research.

claim: In several previous studies, an end-effector irrelevant perturbation was implemented in a bimanual postural task to investigate postural reflex activity.
source: Exceptionally, in several previous studies, an end-effector irrelevant perturbation was implemented in a bimanual postural task to investigate postural reflex activity (Dimitriou et al., 2012; Omrani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: To the authors' knowledge, end-effector irrelevant perturbation has never been used to investigate motor adaptation patterns in a redundant system.
source: However, to our knowledge, such an end-effector irrelevant perturbation has never been used to investigate the motor adaptation pattern in a redundant system.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature.

claim: The task design revealed a novel aspect of motor adaptation to end-effector irrelevant perturbation.
source: Furthermore, as discussed in the next section, our task design revealed a novel aspect of motor adaptation to the end-effector irrelevant perturbation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Adaptation to end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt perturbation was accompanied by an increase in end-effector relevant tip-movement direction error.
source: Unexpectedly, Experiment 2 shows that adaptation to the end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt perturbation was accompanied by an increase in the end-effector relevant tip-movement direction error (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The counterintuitive result can be explained by the constraint of the adaptation pattern along the baseline TMD–STA relationship.
source: This counterintuitive result can be explained by the constraint of the adaptation pattern along the baseline TMD–STA relationship (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental findings based on the baseline relationship.

claim: According to the baseline TMD-STA relationship constraint, CCW (or CW) stick-tilt adaptation should change the tip-movement direction in the CCW (or CW) direction.
source: According to this constraint, CCW (or CW) stick-tilt adaptation should change the tip-movement direction in the CCW (or CW) direction (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the baseline relationship, illustrated in Figure 7c.

claim: The influence of stick-tilt perturbation on tip-movement direction error tended to be more pronounced for participants with a smaller stick-tilt angle at baseline (shallower baseline TMD–STA relationship).
source: The influence of stick-tilt perturbation on tip-movement direction error tended to be more pronounced for participants with a smaller stick-tilt angle at baseline, that is those with a shallower baseline TMD–STA relationship (Figure 7f), further supporting this idea.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The results of Experiment 3 support the existence of interaction between tip-movement and stick-tilt adaptation.
source: The results of Experiment 3 also support the existence of such an interaction between tip-movement and stick-tilt adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of Experiment 3.

claim: When tip-movement and stick-tilt perturbations were imposed simultaneously, the adaptation trajectories on the physical plane were significantly influenced by the perturbation combination patterns.
source: When the tip-movement and stick-tilt perturbations were imposed simultaneously, the adaptation trajectories on the physical plane were significantly influenced by the perturbation combination patterns (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: If the motor system had simply attempted to correct the stick-tilt to reduce the sensory prediction error, the spillover effect on the tip-movement direction would not have been observed.
source: If the motor system had simply attempted to correct the stick-tilt to reduce the sensory prediction error, this spillover effect on the tip-movement direction would not have been observed.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected under an alternative hypothesis.

claim: Given that the baseline TMD–STA relationship reflects motor cost minimization, the motor system is likely attempting to reduce both the sensor prediction error and the motor cost.
source: Given that the baseline TMD–STA relationship (Figure 3a) reflects the motor cost minimization, it is likely that the motor system is attempting to reduce both the sensor prediction error and the motor cost.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in relation to optimization principles.

claim: A possible explanation for why the motor system corrects end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt errors is that the motor system predicts all sensory consequences generated by the action and attempts to correct any differences between predicted and actual sensory information.
source: We speculate that there may be two reasons. First, a possible simple explanation is that the motor system predicts all sensory consequences generated by the action and attempts to correct any differences between the predicted and actual sensory information, even when the task is successfully achieved (Mazzoni and Krakauer, 2006; Schaefer et al., 2012; Morehead et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The correction for end-effector irrelevant stick errors may reflect the motor system's attempt to resolve the dissociation between stick (vision) and hands (proprioception) caused by the perturbation.
source: Similarly, it is possible that the correction for end-effector irrelevant stick errors reflects the motor system's attempt to resolve the dissociation between stick (i.e. vision) and hands (i.e., proprioception) caused by the perturbation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed behavior.

claim: Given that tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle are tightly coupled, the presence of an end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt visual error implies the presence of an end-effector relevant tip-movement direction error.
source: Second, given that tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle are tightly coupled (i.e. the presence of baseline TMD–STA relationship), the presence of an end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt visual error implies the presence of an end-effector relevant tip-movement direction error.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the baseline relationship.

claim: The motor system interprets end-effector irrelevant errors as evidence that end-effector relevant errors have also been produced.
source: In other words, the motor system interprets end-effector irrelevant errors as evidence that end-effector relevant errors have been also produced.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the motor system may process errors in redundant systems.

claim: When sensory information contains noise and/or uncertainty, the reliability of sensory information estimation can be improved by utilizing additional sensory information.
source: When sensory information contains noise and/or uncertainty, the reliability of sensory information estimation can be improved by utilizing additional sensory information (Ernst and Banks, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on multisensory integration.

claim: Utilizing stick-tilt information may be useful for improving the accuracy of the estimation of the tip-movement direction.
source: From this viewpoint, utilizing stick-tilt information may be useful for improving the accuracy of the estimation of the tip-movement direction.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional benefit of using stick-tilt information.

claim: The motor system develops a stereotyped movement pattern through an optimization process that is expressed by a baseline TMD–STA relationship.
source: The motor system develops a stereotyped movement pattern through an optimization process that is expressed by abaseline TMD–STA relationship (gray lines in Figure 10a and Figure 10b).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: The baseline TMD-STA relationship not only dictates how the motor system physically controls the redundant system, but also informs the resulting visual feedback.
source: This relationship not only dictates how the motor system physically controls the redundant system, but also informs the resulting visual feedback.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of the baseline relationship.

claim: When visual perturbations are applied, the motor system tries to eliminate the dissociation of the perturbed state from the original state.
source: When visual perturbations are applied to the tip-movement direction or the stick-tilt angle (bold arrows in Figure 10a), the motor system tries to eliminate the dissociation of the perturbed state from the original state (thin arrows in Figure 10a).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 10a.

claim: The motor system responds to end-effector irrelevant perturbations because the error in the end-effector irrelevant dimension implies the presence of an end-effector relevant error under the condition that stick-tilt angle is tightly coupled with tip-movement direction.
source: It even responds to the end-effector irrelevant perturbation (red and blue arrows in Figure 10a), because the error in the end-effector irrelevant dimension implies the presence of an end-effector relevant error (black dashed arrows in Figure 10a) under the condition that the stick-tilt angle is tightly coupled with the tip-movement direction (i.e. the baseline TMD–STA relationship).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings illustrated in Figure 10a.

claim: The correction patterns predicted by eliminating dissociation are not physically allowed because tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle are physically constrained by the baseline TMD–STA relationship.
source: However, these correction patterns are not physically allowed. Since the tip-movement direction and the stick-tilt angle are physically constrained by the baseline TMD–STA relationship, these correction patterns are biased toward the relationship (bold arrows in Figure 10b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings illustrated in Figure 10b.

claim: The baseline TMD–STA relationship, originally developed to control the redundant system, also plays a crucial role in how the motor system should implicitly respond to visual errors and correct physical movement.
source: In summary, this study shows that the baseline TMD–STA relationship, originally developed to control the redundant system, also plays a crucial role for the motor system in how it should implicitly respond to the visual errors and how it should correct the physical movement.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings provide a novel framework for understanding how the motor system learns to control the redundant system when encountering visual errors.
source: This idea provides a novel framework for understanding how the motor system leans to control the redundant system when encountering visual errors.
evidence: This is a claim about the theoretical contribution of the study.

claim: A total of 72 healthy adults (25 females and 47 males, aged 22.1±2.5 years old) participated in the study.
source: A total of 72 healthy adults (25 females and 47 males, aged 22.1±2.5 years old; mean ± SD) participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics.

claim: All participants were right-handed according to their laterality score (83.3±13.7) obtained using the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: All the participants were right-handed according to their laterality score (83.3±13.7; mean ± SD) obtained using the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971).
evidence: This describes participant characteristics based on a standardized assessment.

claim: Participants performed reaching movements using a virtual stick displayed on a horizontal screen with both handles of a manipulandum (KINARM End-Point Lab).
source: The participants performed reaching movements using a virtual stick displayed on a horizontal screen with both handles of a manipulandum (KINARM End-Point Lab; Kinarm, Kingston, Canada; Scott, 1999; Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus.

claim: The screen prevented participants from directly seeing their arms and handles.
source: This screen prevented the participants from directly seeing their arms and handles, and displayed a start position, a target (1.4 cm in diameter), and a virtual stick (length: 40 cm, width: 0.5 cm).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: The distance between the handles was fixed using a strong elastic force produced by the manipulandum (spring constant = 2000 N/m).
