source: The distance between the handles was fixed using a strong elastic force produced by the manipulandum (spring constant = 2000 N/m).
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus configuration.

claim: The positions and velocities of the hands were analogue/digitally converted at 1.129 kHz and then recorded at 1 kHz for offline analysis.
source: The positions and velocities of the hands were analogue/digitally converted at 1.129 kHz and then recorded at 1 kHz for offline analysis.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: All experiments comprised a baseline phase (360 trials) followed by an adaptation phase (240 trials).
source: All the experiments (Experiments 1–3) comprised a baseline phase (360 trials) followed by an adaptation phase (240 trials).
evidence: This describes the experimental structure.

claim: Participants were instructed to maintain the peak velocities of the tip as constant as possible across trials.
source: The participants were instructed to maintain the peak velocities of the tip as constant as possible across the trials.
evidence: This describes the task instructions.

claim: When the tip reached the target, a feedback message 'fast' or 'slow' was presented if the peak movement speed was higher or lower than the range of 300–450 mm/s.
source: When the tip reached the target, a feedback message, 'fast' or 'slow', was presented on the monitor if the peak movement speed was higher or lower than the range of 300–450 mm/s, respectively.
evidence: This describes the feedback provided to participants.

claim: In Experiment 1A, the tip-movement direction on the monitor was gradually rotated CCW direction around the starting position by 1° per trial up to 30°.
source: In Experiment 1 A, the tip-movement direction on the monitor was gradually rotated CCW direction around the starting position by 1° per trial up to 30° (Figure 4a).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 1A.

claim: In Experiment 1A, the stick-tilt angle remained unchanged (identical to the angle of the line connecting both hands).
source: The stick-tilt angle remained unchanged (i.e., the stick-tilt angle was identical to the angle of the line connecting both hands).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 1A.

claim: In Experiment 1A, participants did not perceive the presence of rotation and the adaptation was considered to be dominated by the implicit process.
source: In Experiment 1 A, participants did not perceive the presence of rotation and the adaptation was considered to be dominated by the implicit process.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental manipulation.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the 30° visual rotation was abruptly applied to the tip-movement direction, which allowed participants to use an explicit strategy.
source: On the other hand, in Experiment 1B, the 30° visual rotation was abruptly applied to the tip-movement direction, which allowed them to use an explicit strategy.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 1B.

claim: In Experiment 2, the stick-tilt angle on the monitor was rotated around the right tip in the CW direction (E2CW group, N=10) or in the CCW direction (E2CCW group, N=10).
source: Experiment 2 (N=20) examined whether the motor system was indifferent to end-effector irrelevant perturbations (stick-tilt perturbations). The stick-tilt angle on the monitor was rotated around the right tip in the CW direction (E2CW group, N=10) or in the CCW direction (E2CCW group, N=10).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the perturbations did not affect the tip-movement direction.
source: Notably, these perturbations did not affect the tip-movement direction.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the experimental manipulation in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, during each reaching trial, the stick-tilt angle increased from 0° to 6° in proportion to the distance of the tip position from the starting point (0.6°/cm).
source: During each reaching trial, the stick-tilt angle increased from 0° to 6° in proportion to the distance of the tip position from the starting point (0.6°/cm; Figure 6a).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants did not notice any perturbations during the experiment.
source: Participants did not notice any perturbations during the experiment.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental manipulation.

claim: In Experiment 3, both tip-movement and stick-tilt perturbations were simultaneously imposed.
source: In Experiment 3 (N=20), to examine how end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt perturbations influenced adaptation to end-effector relevant tip perturbations, both tip-movement and stick-tilt perturbations were simultaneously imposed (Figure 8a).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 3.

claim: The procedure for applying tip and stick-tilt perturbations in Experiment 3 was the same as in Experiment 1A and Experiment 2, respectively.
source: The procedure for applying tip and stick-tilt perturbations was the same as in Experiment 1 A and Experiment 2, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, participants did not notice perturbations during the experiment.
source: The participants did not notice perturbations during the experiment.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental manipulation.

claim: Data analyses were performed using MATLAB R2023a.
source: Data analyses were performed using MATLAB R2023a (MathWorks, Natick, Massachusetts, USA).
evidence: This describes the data analysis software.

claim: The behavioral data were low-pass filtered (10 Hz, fourth-order Butterworth filter).
source: The behavioral data were low-pass filtered (10 Hz, fourth-order Butterworth filter).
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: The tip-movement direction was calculated as the movement direction of the tip relative to the horizontal direction.
source: The tip-movement direction was calculated as the movement direction of the tip relative to the horizontal direction (Figure 3a).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The stick-tilt angle was defined as the tilting angle of the stick from the horizontal line.
source: The stick-tilt angle was defined as the tilting angle of the stick from the horizontal line (Figure 3a).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: Positive values for both tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle were defined as the degree to the CCW direction.
source: Positive values for both parameters were defined as the degree to the CCW direction.
evidence: This describes the data analysis convention.

claim: Unless otherwise noted, the tip-movement direction and the stick-tilt angle at the tip's peak velocity were used to evaluate the feedforward motor commands.
source: Unless otherwise noted, the tip-movement direction and the stick-tilt angle at the tip's peak velocity were used to evaluate the feedforward motor commands.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach.

claim: Statistical evaluations were conducted using t-tests, correlation analyses, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, and MANOVA using MATLAB, JASP, and R studio.
source: To statistically evaluate the behavioral data, we conducted t-tests, correlation analyses, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, and MANOVA using MATLAB, the software package JASP (http://jasp-stats.org), and R studio.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis methods.
